title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I will look at median gross rent in Illinois. I will explore which communities are measured the most and least reliably, and what impacts that could have on public policy.

How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM  popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 17001 Adams County, Illinois        826     43 65166    NA
2 17003 Alexander County, Illinois    540    214  5042    NA
3 17005 Bond County, Illinois         735     34 16627    NA
4 17007 Boone County, Illinois       1011     71 53316    NA
5 17009 Brown County, Illinois        724    119  6320    NA
6 17011 Bureau County, Illinois       838     66 33027    NA



county_wide <- county_wide |> 
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) |> 
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide |> 
  group_by(reliability) |> 
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         38        299458.
2 Low confidence          10          7787.
3 Moderate                54         22877.


[The average population of a “high confidence” county is about 299458, a “moderate confidence” county is about 22877, and a “low confidence” county is about 7787. This indicates that counties with lower average populations tend to have less reliable, or uncertain, data regarding median gross rent.]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy

Which communities in your state do we know the least about? The counties in Illinois that we know the least about are Alexander, Brown, Gallatin, Hamilton, Hardin, Johnson, Massac, Menard, Pope, and Schuyler. All 10 of these counties are classified as “low confidence” reliability due to their large percentage of margin of error.
Why? The American Community Survey (ACS) is based on data that is sampled from the population, rather than surveying every single person like the Decennial Census. Counties with smaller populations will produce a smaller sample size, thus likely resulting in more uncertainty than a large county with a large sample size. When analyzing statistics, a smaller sample size will almost always have a larger margin of error than a larger sample size. This uncertainty is what causes these small counties to have “low confidence” reliability.
What could go wrong? If a state agency were to allocate resources using this variable, they may over-allocate or under-allocate to any of the 10 “low confidence” counties. While over-allocating may waste limited resources and taxpayer dollars, under-allocating can leave many vulnerable people in need. Conversely, it is likely that their allocations for larger counties, which typically fall in the “high confidence” reliability due to their small margins of error, will be accurate. Treating every county’s number as equally certain is inherently unfair to small counties.

[Upon learning how the ACS operates, I was naively shocked to find out that the data is extrapolated from a much smaller sample size, not the entire population. In my childhood, I imagined government workers going door to door with detailed paper surveys that they would then spend months logging into a large complex computer software. After Friday’s class, I found myself questioning the ethics of creating policy, even if it is positive, based off of data that may not be entirely comprehensive or representative of the people which whom it will affect. After completing this assignment, I am even further convinced that there must be another way to understand people, where they live, and how they live. I think that this is where I see community engagement operating most effectively. Bridging the gap between what is “data” and what is “reality”. Although data analytics can be excellent at analyzing large overarching trends, I think in some ways it fails to get as fine tuned as one would hope, at least regarding census data. As spatial analysts, we have a responsibility to understand and communicate not just the great potential of data analysis, but also it’s limits.]

title: Verify the Claim: New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct the Data
Variables Used
B17001_001E : total population for whom poverty status is determined - This will be used to determine the poverty rate. Using “B01003_001E : total population” would not be accurate because the ACS excludes some people from their poverty rate calculation if they are determined inapplicable.
B17001_002E : total population below the poverty level - This will be used to determine the poverty rate. Dividing the total population below the poverty level by the total population applicable will give me the poverty rate.
B17001_001M : MOE for the total - The margin of error will allow me to determine the certainity of the statistical outcome.
B17001_002M : MOE for below poverty - The margin of error will allow me to determine the certainty of the statistical outcome.
I used the 2006-2010 ACS5 survey data to represent the 2010 data mentioned in the article, and the 2013-2017 ACS5 survey data to represent the 2017 data mentioned in the article. Although the article mentions some data from the 2016 ACS1 report, it’s main claim compares the change in the poverty rate from 2010 to 2017. The two periods do not overlap.
I assumed that the article correctly calculated the poverty rate by using “total population for whom poverty status is determined” rather than just “total population”. I myself did not realize that this is the correct way to calculate the poverty rate before reading this on the US Census Bureau website.



Part 2 — Test (code plus interpretation)
Data Setup


Show code
library (tidycensus)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(gt)




Show code
vars <- c(
total = "B17001_001",
below = "B17001_002"
)

acs_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output ="wide"
)

acs_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


Compute the Poverty Rate


Show code
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_rt = belowE / totalE)
acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_rt = belowE / totalE)


Compute the Margin of Error (MOE)


Show code
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_moe = moe_prop(
  belowE,
  totalE,
  belowM,
  totalM
))

acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_moe = moe_prop(
  belowE,
  totalE,
  belowM,
  totalM
))


Compute the coefficient of variation


Show code
acs_2010 <- mutate(acs_2010, poverty_cv = ((poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rt) * 100)
acs_2017 <- mutate(acs_2017, poverty_cv = ((poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rt) * 100)


Flag reliability using the Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds: CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.


Show code
reliability_table_2010 <- acs_2010 |> 
  mutate(
    dot = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ "",
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "🟢",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag = case_when(
      is.na(poverty_cv) ~ "Not available",
      poverty_cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      poverty_cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(poverty_cv)) |> 
  select(
    dot,
    NAME,
    totalE,
    belowE,
    poverty_rt,
    poverty_moe,
    poverty_cv,
    flag
  )

reliability_table_2010 |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(totalE, belowE),
    decimals = 0
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_rt,
    decimals = 1,
    scale_by = 100
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_moe,
    decimals = 3
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = poverty_cv,
    decimals = 1
  ) |> 
  cols_label(
    dot = "",
    NAME = "Census Tract",
    totalE = "Population",
    belowE = "Below Poverty",
    poverty_rt = "Poverty Rate (%)",
    poverty_moe = "MOE",

Part 3 — Adjudicate
The analysis supports the article’s claim that that poverty rates changed in some Philadelphia census tracts between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS periods.
That being said, this analysis cannot be used to determine a large majority of the claims in the article. This is for a variety of reasons but mainly being that the data only represents the poverty rate and does not indicate other factors such as the depth of poverty, the race associated with each tract, or the reason for which an individual may be in poverty. For this reason, claims such as 50% or more of people in poverty are living below the federal poverty rate, and a lack of employment, drug addiction, immigration or retirement are the main causes for increased poverty rates, cannot be supported.
Additionally, the article details poverty at the neighborhood scale whereas the census collects data by tracts, thus also making it difficult to draw sound data-based conclusions. Claims such as certain neighborhoods are becoming destinations for impoverished households to move into and poverty rates in majority-white neighborhoods are dramatically increasing cannot be fully determined since a single neighborhood is typically comprised of multiple tracts. Furthermore, census tracts do not fit neatly into a neighborhood boundary (which itself is up for dispute), but rather can cross and cut through neighborhoods in a variety of ways.
Finally, most of the claims in the article are anecdotal. Although they are presented alongside the census data and by seemingly reputable sources - food pantry directors, community organizers, social workers, etc. - this does not mean that the census data directly supports these claims.
In general, the ACS data supports evidence of change in some tracts, but not the causal explanations offered for why those changes occurred.



Part 4 — Rewrite
A new five-year federal survey shows that poverty rates changed in some Philadelphia neighborhoods between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 periods. In my analysis, 63 of 376 tracts had poverty-rate changes that were statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90 percent confidence level, while 313 did not. The data therefore shows that poverty shifted significantly in some parts of the city, but not all of it. It also does not establish why those changes occurred. The survey cannot determine whether changes resulted from the Great Recession, unemployment, migration, evictions, opioid addiction, retirement, or other factors suggested by residents and community leaders. Those explanations require additional evidence beyond the ACS poverty estimates. The five-year ACS also carries margins of error, making it important to distinguish measurable changes from differences that may reflect sampling uncertainty.

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 0.5) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 238


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.479  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.

fatal_proj <- st_transform(fatal_crashes, 2272)

# join each violation point to a census tract

  violations_proj,
  tracts_proj["GEOID"],
  join = st_within
)

# count violations in each tract
violation_counts <- violations_joined |> 
  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  count(GEOID, name = "parking_violations")

# add counts to tracts and replace missing counts with zero
tracts_proj <- tracts_proj |> 
  left_join(violation_counts, by = "GEOID") |> 
  mutate(parking_violations = coalesce(parking_violations, 0L))

# assign crashes to tracts
crashes_joined <- st_join(
  fatal_proj,
  tracts_proj["GEOID"],
  join = st_within
)

# count crashes per tract
crash_counts <- crashes_joined |> 
  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  count(GEOID, name = "fatal_crashes")

# calculate tract area in square kilometers and density
tracts_proj <- tracts_proj |> 
  left_join(crash_counts, by = "GEOID") |> 
  mutate(
    fatal_crashes = coalesce(fatal_crashes, 0L),
    area_sqkm = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6,
    crash_density = fatal_crashes / area_sqkm
  )

# remove crashes with missing or empty geometry

  !st_is_empty(fatal_proj) &
    !is.na(st_geometry(fatal_proj)),
]

# find nearest crash for each centroid
nearest_crash <- st_nearest_feature(
  tract_centroids,
  fatal_valid
)

  st_distance(
    tract_centroids,
    fatal_valid[nearest_crash, ],
    by_element = TRUE
  )
)

model_log <- model_log |> 
  add_row(
    model = "m2",
    added = "parking_violations",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts_proj),
    notes = "Count of parking violations within each census tract"
  )

  add_row(
    model = "m3",
    added = "crash_density",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts_proj),
    notes = "Fatal crashes per square kilometer"
  )

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)

5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))

Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.
